R. Ambedkar, M.A., Ph.D. (Columbia), D.Sc. (London), Bar-at-Law.

pages.label: On caste as a division of labourers

passages.text: Caste is not just a division of labour, it is a division of labourers. Civilised society undoubtedly needs division of labour — but in no civilised society is division of labour accompanied by this unnatural division of labourers into watertight compartments.
passages.note: Widely reproduced formulation — wording to be verified against the printed edition before production use.

passages.text: The address goes on to examine how caste poisons every relation of life — education, employment, marriage — and why social reform must precede, not follow, political reform.
passages.note: Editorial summary paragraph, curator-reviewed for the demo corpus.

pages.ocr: Caste is not just a divison of labour, it is a division of labourers. Civilised society undoubtedly needs division of labour - but in no civilised society is division of labour acompanied by this unnatural division of labourers into watertight compart ments.

pages.label: On remedies

passages.text: The concluding section weighs the remedies proposed for dissolving caste — inter-dining, inter-marriage, and the destruction of the religious sanction behind caste — and argues that political and economic change alone cannot dissolve it.
passages.note: Paraphrase-safe summary; exact quotation pending curator verification against the printed edition.

pages.ocr: The concluding seciton weighs the remedies proposed for disolving caste - inter-dining, inter-marraige, and the destruciton of the religious sanction behind caste - and argues that political and economic change alone cannot dissolve it.

items.title: Constituent Assembly Debates — 26 November 1949
items.creator: Constituent Assembly of India
items.speaker: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
items.sourceName: Parliament Digital Library — Constituent Assembly Debates
items.desc: The closing day of the Drafting Committee’s work: the Assembly adopts the Constitution, and its Chairman delivers the speech every civics textbook quotes.

pages.label: Session record

passages.text: The Constituent Assembly met in the Constitution Hall, New Delhi, on Saturday, 26 November 1949, and proceeded to consider and adopt the Constitution of India — the culmination of two years, eleven months and eighteen days of drafting.
passages.note: Session context, curator-reviewed for the demo corpus.

pages.ocr: The Constituent Assembly met in the Constition Hall, New Delhi, on Saturday, 26 November 1949, and proceeded to consider and adopt the Constitution of India - the culmination of two years, eleven months and eighteen days of drafting.

pages.label: The closing speech

passages.text: Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated. We must realise that our people have yet to learn it. Democracy in India is only a top-dressing on an Indian soil which is essentially undemocratic.
passages.note: Widely reproduced excerpt — wording to be verified against the printed Lok Sabha Secretariat edition before production use.

passages.text: However good a Constitution may be, if those who are implementing it are not good, it will prove to be bad. However bad a Constitution may be, if those implementing it are good, it will prove to be good.
passages.note: Widely reproduced excerpt — wording to be verified against the printed edition before production use.

passages.text: The speech closes with the warning that on 26 January 1950 India would enter “a life of contradictions” — political equality sitting atop social and economic inequality — and that the sooner this contradiction is removed, the better for the country.
passages.note: Contextual summary, curator-reviewed for the demo corpus.

pages.ocr: Constitutional morality is not a natural sentimant. It has to be cultivated. We must realise that our people have yet to learn it. Democracy in India is only a top-dressing on an Indian soil which is essentially undemocratic.

pages.label: Adoption of the motion

passages.text: The motion that the Constitution, as settled by the Assembly, be passed was put and adopted. The date of commencement was fixed by separate resolution: 26 January 1950 — the twentieth anniversary of Purna Swaraj Day.
passages.note: Record summary, curator-reviewed for the demo corpus.

pages.ocr: The motion that the Constitution, as settled by the Assembly, be passed was put and adopted. The date of commencemant was fixed by seperate resolution: 26 January 1950 - the twentiith anniversary of Purna Swaraj Day.

pages.label: “As to the charge of plagiarism…”

passages.text: As to the accusation that the Draft Constitution has reproduced a good part of the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, I make no apologies. There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing. It involves no plagiarism. Nobody holds any patent rights in the fundamental ideas of a Constitution.
passages.note: Widely reproduced excerpt — wording to be verified against the printed edition before production use.

events.title: A child of Mhow
events.text: Bhimrao Ramji Sakpal is born at Mhow in the Central Provinces — present-day Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, Madhya Pradesh — the youngest of Ramji Maloji Sakpal’s children.

events.title: Across the oceans
events.text: A scholarship from the State of Baroda takes the young Ambedkar to Columbia University, New York — where John Dewey’s seminars leave a lifelong mark. Degrees and the Bar follow at Columbia, the LSE and Gray’s Inn.

events.title: The Mooknayak speaks
events.text: The first issue of the Marathi weekly Mooknayak appears in Bombay, launched with the support of Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur — a press of their own for those long denied one.

events.title: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha
events.text: The association for the education and uplift of the excluded is founded in Bombay — running hostels, libraries and classes where the state would not.

events.title: Mahad — water for all
events.text: At the Chavadar tank in Mahad, thousands assert the right to take water from a public tank. The Mahad Satyagraha becomes a founding act of the movement for civic equality; December brings the burning of the Manusmriti as a symbol of rejected authority.

events.title: Kalaram temple entry
events.text: The satyagraha to enter the Kalaram temple at Nashik begins — a disciplined campaign for the right to worship, facing obstruction for years.

events.title: The Poona Pact
events.text: Signed at Yerwada after Mahatma Gandhi’s fast against separate electorates: reserved seats within the general electorate replace the Communal Award’s separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

events.title: Annihilation of Caste
events.text: The undelivered Lahore address is published by its author, with the organisers’ correspondence — the sharpest single critique of caste in twentieth-century Indian letters.

events.title: The Federation is founded
events.text: The All-India Scheduled Castes Federation is formed at Nagpur, carrying the movement into all-India politics — successor to the Independent Labour Party of 1936.

events.title: Chairman of the Drafting Committee
events.text: Days after Independence — and now Law Minister in free India’s first cabinet — Dr. Ambedkar is elected Chairman of the Constituent Assembly’s Drafting Committee.

events.title: “…adopt, enact and give to ourselves”
events.text: The Constituent Assembly adopts the Constitution. The Chairman’s closing speech warns that democracy remains “a top-dressing” until social and economic equality catches up with the ballot.

events.title: The Republic is born
events.text: The Constitution comes into force — the date chosen to honour Purna Swaraj Day, 26 January 1930. India becomes a sovereign democratic republic.

events.title: Dhamma Deeksha, Nagpur
events.text: At Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, Dr. Ambedkar receives the Three Jewels and Five Precepts — joined in conversion by hundreds of thousands of followers.

events.title: Mahaparinirvana
events.text: Dr. Ambedkar passes away at his Delhi residence. Chaitya Bhoomi, his cremation site in Dadar, becomes a place of remembrance for millions.

ask_set.answer: In his closing speech to the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar observed that constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment — it has to be cultivated — and warned that democracy in India was “only a top-dressing on an Indian soil which is essentially undemocratic” until equality reached social and economic life.

Annihilation of Caste (1936) is the presidential address withdrawn under pressure from its host organisation and then published by Dr. Ambedkar himself. It argues that caste is not merely a division of labour but a division of labourers, and that no remedy succeeds without destroying the religious sanction that upholds caste.

The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949, after two years, eleven months and eighteen days of drafting. It came into force on 26 January 1950 — the date chosen to honour Purna Swaraj Day of 26 January 1930.

The Poona Pact of 24 September 1932 was signed at Yerwada following Mahatma Gandhi’s fast against the Communal Award’s separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats within the general electorate — a settlement whose terms shaped later safeguards, addressed again in States and Minorities (1947).

On 14 October 1956 at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, Dr. Ambedkar publicly received the Three Jewels and the Five Precepts, and was joined in conversion by hundreds of thousands of followers. Nagpur was chosen for its resonance with this land’s Buddhist past. The archive holds a modern narrated account of that day — labelled MODERN NARRATION, not an authentic recording.

26 January marks the day the Constitution came into force in 1950. The date was deliberately chosen to honour Purna Swaraj Day — 26 January 1930 — when the Indian National Congress first pledged complete independence. The illuminated manuscript of the Constitution, calligraphed and painted by artists of Santiniketan, is held as one of the Republic’s treasures.

Mooknayak — “the hero of the mute” — was the Marathi weekly launched in Bombay on 31 January 1920 under the editorship of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, with the support of Chhatrapati Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur. It gave the movement its first press of its own. The first issue is held in the archive as a scan with reviewed Marathi text; its full translation is pending review.

The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly held its first sitting on 29 August 1947 and elected Dr. B. R. Ambedkar — then Law Minister — as its Chairman. The Committee produced the Draft Constitution placed before the Assembly on 4 November 1948.
